title: Post-Course Portfolio: Real-Time Online Tic-Tac-Toe
descriptionMarkdown:
# Real-Time Online Tic-Tac-Toe

## Position in the curriculum

Post-course portfolio: build after finishing the full curriculum through the final capstone. This is the catalog's introduction to real-time, bidirectional communication, deliberately started with the simplest possible game so the WebSocket plumbing is the thing being learned, not the game logic.

## What is graded, and what is external

This project has a dedicated, automatically-graded checkpoint: **`tic-tac-toe-checkpoint`** ("Turn-validated tic-tac-toe engine"), a pure in-memory `TicTacToeEngine.run(String input)` program implementing exactly the turn-validation and win/draw-detection core. Passing its hidden tests proves your game logic is correct, independent of any real WebSocket transport.

The real-time delivery of moves over a WebSocket connection, matchmaking into a session, and disconnect handling are external and self-reviewed.

## Beyond what the lessons taught

WebSockets and Spring's `spring-websocket`/STOMP support are not covered by the 25-chapter curriculum, which teaches request-response HTTP (Chapter 18) and in-process concurrency (Chapter 17) but not a persistent, bidirectional server connection. Treat learning Spring's WebSocket support as required, deliberate self-directed research for this project, using the official Spring Framework reference documentation as your primary source.

## Architecture overview

```text
GameWebSocketHandler            <- accepts connections, matches players into GameSession, routes move messages
GameSession                      <- your checkpoint's turn/win/draw rules, reshaped as a stateful session object
SessionRegistry                  <- in-memory map of active sessions, guarded against concurrent move handling
```

## Build it as vertical slices

1. **Slice 1 — port the checkpoint logic into a session object.** Carry your turn-validation and win/draw rules into `GameSession`, unit tests unchanged.
2. **Slice 2 — a bare WebSocket echo endpoint.** Get a connection accepted and a message round-tripped before adding any game logic, so transport and game logic are debugged separately.
3. **Slice 3 — a two-player queue and session handoff.** Match the first two connecting players into one `GameSession`; broadcast the initial empty board to both.
4. **Slice 4 — moves, validated and broadcast.** Route an incoming move message through your ported `GameSession` logic; broadcast the resulting board (or win/draw) to both connected players; reject an illegal move without corrupting the broadcast state.
5. **Slice 5 — disconnect handling.** Implement and document your chosen policy (forfeit after a grace period, or pause-and-allow-reconnection).

## Common pitfalls

- **Trusting a client to declare its own win.** Detect win/draw server-side from the authoritative board, exactly as the checkpoint's own `WIN`/`DRAW` output already does.
- **Applying two near-simultaneous move messages without synchronizing access to the shared session state.** Use the same guarded-shared-state discipline as Chapter 17's lab; exactly one of two racing moves for the same session must be applied.
- **Broadcasting a corrupted or partially-updated board after rejecting an illegal move.** An invalid move must leave the broadcast state identical to before the attempt, exactly as the checkpoint's own contract requires.
- **Leaving a disconnect unhandled, so the remaining player's client hangs forever.** Pick and document one policy; an undocumented default is not acceptable.

## How to self-test what the checkpoint cannot reach

- Fire two near-simultaneous move messages at the same session from two clients and confirm exactly one is applied.
- Play a full game to a win via two real WebSocket client connections and confirm both clients receive the identical final board.
- Disconnect one client mid-game and confirm your documented policy actually fires within its stated time bound.

## Required evidence

- A concurrency test simulating two near-simultaneous move messages for the same session, confirming exactly one is applied and the other is rejected as "not your turn" or "cell occupied," never both silently applied.
- A full win/draw detection test suite covering every winning line and a genuine draw.
- A test (or documented manual walkthrough) of the disconnect-handling behavior you chose.
- A test confirming an illegal move (wrong turn, occupied cell, game already over) is rejected without corrupting the board state broadcast to the other player.
- A short write-up of your WebSocket message protocol (the shape of a move message and a broadcast update), since no lesson defined one for you.

## Review and completion

A reviewer opens two browser tabs (or two WebSocket client sessions) as the two players, plays a complete game to a win, then starts a second game and has one player disconnect mid-game, expecting your documented disconnect behavior to actually occur rather than the server hanging or crashing.
learningObjectives: Complete the graded turn-validated tic-tac-toe engine checkpoint and carry its verified rules into a real WebSocket session
Research and apply a real-time communication mechanism (WebSockets) beyond what the lessons covered
Protect shared, mutable game state from a race between two near-simultaneous client messages
Validate every incoming move server-side rather than trusting client-reported game outcomes
Design and document a message protocol for a real-time feature no lesson specified
